blocks.text: Let the application load data into a cache on demand and keep the database as the source of truth.

On a read the application checks the cache first. On a **miss** it reads the database, stores the result with a **TTL**, and returns it. On a write it updates the database and **invalidates** the cached entry. The cache never talks to the database itself; the application owns both sides.

items: **Read:** hit returns; miss loads, stores, returns.
**Write:** update the source, then delete the cached copy.
**Expiry:** a TTL bounds how stale a missed invalidation can be.

blocks.text: The cache can briefly disagree with the database. Cache-aside gives eventual consistency, not a transaction across both.

Check the entry and its expiry against the injected clock. Only a present row is cached. A miss falls through to the store and fills the cache.
Write the database first, then evict. Evicting rather than updating the cache avoids racing writers leaving an older value cached.

blocks.text: A product catalog read by every page view.

A catalog service reads product details from PostgreSQL, thousands of times a second for a small hot set. Product data changes a few times a day. Putting Redis in front with a ten-minute TTL cuts database load by orders of magnitude. The price-update job writes the database and then deletes the key, so the next read reloads the fresh value. A restart of Redis only causes a temporary rise in database reads.
Payoff: hot reads come from memory, and the cache can be lost at any time without losing data.

lists.title: Use when
items: Reads far outnumber writes and a small hot set dominates.
The data tolerates seconds or minutes of staleness.
The cache may be cold or lost without data loss.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Reads must always see the latest write, such as balances.
Access is uniformly spread, so hit rates stay low.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Stampede: many readers miss on a popular key and hit the database together.
Race: a reader loads old data, a writer evicts, and the reader then caches the stale row.
Absent rows never cached, so repeated lookups for missing keys hit the database.
No TTL: a missed eviction stays wrong forever.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Caching to hide a missing index or an N+1 query.
Caching entities that are written as often as read.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Caffeine's `LoadingCache` gives per-key single-flight loading, so only one thread loads a missing key.
`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` is fine for in-process caches, but keep slow loads out of it.

rows.difference: Cache-aside often lives inside a repository, so callers see one data-access seam and never the cache.
A caching proxy is transparent to the caller and the cache sits in the call path. In cache-aside, application code explicitly manages the cache.
A decorating repository can add cache-aside behavior without changing callers. Read-through and write-through caches move the loading into the cache itself.
Event sourcing stores events as the truth and derives state; a cache is a disposable copy of state the database already holds.
Cache-aside reduces calls; retry and breaker cover the calls that still reach the database.

entries.name: Second-level cache
entries.detail: Entity caches filled on a load and invalidated on update, through JCache or Infinispan providers.

entries.name: EXPIRE and SET with EX
entries.detail: Native TTLs make time-bounded entries cheap, the usual store behind cache-aside.

exercises.prompt: Explain the read and write paths of cache-aside, why writes evict instead of update, and the main risk.

modelAnswer.text: Reads check the cache, load from the database on a miss and store with a TTL. Writes update the database and then delete the cached entry, because updating the cache can leave an older value after racing writers. The risks are brief staleness and stampedes on a hot key.

keyPoints: The application manages the cache; the database is the truth
Read: check, load on miss, fill with TTL
Write: update the database, then evict
Eviction avoids races that updating can cause
